title: What is async/await and how does it relate to Promises?
description: Syntactic sugar over promises: how await suspends without blocking, error propagation, concurrency with Promise.all, and common pitfalls.

data.text: **Question:** What is async/await and how does it relate to Promises?

`async/await` is **syntax for working with Promises** that makes asynchronous code read like synchronous code. A function marked `async` always returns a Promise (its return value is wrapped; a thrown error becomes a rejected promise). Inside it, `await <promise>` **suspends the function** until the promise settles, then yields its value — or throws if it rejected. Crucially, awaiting does **not block the thread**: the event loop stays free to run other work; only this function's continuation is paused. It's built into the language on top of the promise machinery — `await x` is equivalent to `x.then(...)` under the hood, with proper microtask scheduling.

**Core semantics:**
- `async function f() { return 1 }` → `f()` is a resolved promise with value 1; `throw` → rejected promise
- `await p` pauses only the async function; the microtask queue continues processing other work
- `await` on a non-promise value just yields it on the next microtask tick (slight timing difference vs sync code)
- Async functions can be awaited themselves — awaiting an async function awaits its returned promise

**Error handling:**
- try/catch works exactly like sync code — `await api.get()` inside try, catch the rejection
- Unhandled rejections: forgetting await or catch means the rejection hits `unhandledrejection`
- `throw` inside async → rejection; rejections inside `.then` callbacks → caught by the next `.catch`

**Concurrency — the classic pitfall:**
- Sequential `await` in a loop: one request per round trip — slow. `for (const id of ids) results.push(await fetchOne(id))` waits N times
- Fix with **Promise.all** (parallel) or **Promise.allSettled** (tolerate failures): `const results = await Promise.all(ids.map(fetchOne))`
- When order matters, `Promise.all` preserves input order in results
- Start promises **before** awaiting them to overlap independent work: `const a = getA(); const b = getB(); const [x, y] = await Promise.all([a, b]);`

**Other details:**
- Top-level `await` is legal in ES modules (and thus in modern bundlers/Node ESM) — no async wrapper needed
- `await` inside `.then(callback)` delays by an extra microtask vs plain `.then`
- Cancellation: promises can't be cancelled — pass an AbortController signal (fetch supports it)
- For streams/iteration of async sequences, `for await...of` iterates async iterables

data.title: Sequential vs parallel, and error propagation
Await is a pause button, not a stop sign
data.text: While your async function waits, the JavaScript thread is fully available: timers fire, other promises resolve, UI stays responsive. That's also why mixing await with shared mutable state (module-level variables) creates races — other code runs during the pause.

Interviewers want to assess:
- async functions always return promises; await suspends the function, not the thread
- try/catch equivalence with .then/.catch
- The sequential-await vs Promise.all performance insight (usually the real question)
- Practical knowledge: top-level await, AbortController, unhandled rejections

items: Awaiting in a for loop for independent requests — serializing what could be parallel
Forgetting await: `const data = fetch(...)` then using data — you get a promise
Fire-and-forget async in event handlers without catch — silent unhandled rejections
Awaiting inside .then and assuming same timing — extra microtask tick
Assuming await can block or cancel — promises are not cancellable; use signals
Creating races: awaiting between read and write of shared state others can touch

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: async functions return promises; await suspends only that function
try/catch handles rejections exactly like sync exceptions
Independent awaits belong in Promise.all, not serial loops
Promises aren't cancellable — carry AbortController signals
data.takeaway: async/await makes async code legible, but it doesn't make it sequential — launch independent work first, then await the results together.
